options.content:
#### What this dashboard answers
Companion uses Go's `database/sql` connection pool to talk to PostgreSQL. This dashboard answers four questions, top to bottom:

| Section | Question | Look at |
|---|---|---|
| **Overview** | Is anything wrong right now? | Coloured tiles: green = fine, orange = watch, red = act |
| **Saturation** | Is any pod running out of connections? | Busiest pod, not the average |
| **Contention** | Are requests actually waiting? This is the user-visible impact. | Waits/s and the average wait time |
| **Connection lifecycle** | Is the pool churning (opening/closing connections too often)? | Estimated connection lifetime |

#### Triage flow
1. **Red saturation, no waits:** the pool is busy but still keeping up. Plan capacity before it starts queueing.
2. **Waits > 0:** requests block until a connection frees up, and that time adds directly to request latency. Then check *who* is saturated:
   - **every pod** → capacity problem: raise `SetMaxOpenConns` or scale out, *within* the PostgreSQL `max_connections` budget;
   - **a single pod** → local problem: slow queries, long transactions, uneven load balancing, or a **connection leak** (`rows`/`tx` not closed). A leak looks like *in use* stuck near *max* while traffic is low.
3. **Short estimated lifetime (seconds rather than minutes):** churn. Each new connection costs a TCP + TLS + auth handshake on PostgreSQL. Review `SetConnMaxLifetime`, `SetConnMaxIdleTime` and `SetMaxIdleConns`.

#### Key relationships
- `open = in use + idle` and `open ≤ max open` on each pod.
- `sum(open)` over all pods (plus every other client) must fit under PostgreSQL `max_connections`.
- `max open = 0` means **unlimited** in Go. Saturation can't be computed then, and the pool can exhaust the database. Treat it as a misconfiguration.
- Counters (`*_total`) reset when a process restarts. `rate()` handles this, so the graphs stay correct across deployments.

#### Variables
- **Application:** value of the application label on the metrics.
- **Pod:** filter on one or more pods. Each pod runs its own Companion process, hence its own connection pool.
- **Scope:** every query is restricted to `kube_pod_label_component="companion-service"`.
- Hidden setting (*Settings → Variables*): `app_label`, name of the label set from `LabelApplication` in the code (default `application`).

*Every panel has a ⓘ tooltip explaining what it shows, what healthy looks like and what to do when it isn't.*

panels.title: Overview: is the pool healthy right now?
Saturation (busiest pod)
panels.description:
**What:** highest `in use / max open` ratio across the selected pods.

**Healthy:** below 70 %. Above 90 %, new queries on that pod are about to queue.

**Why the max:** each pod has its own pool, so one saturated pod hurts its users even if the average looks fine.

Pods with `max open = 0` (unlimited) are excluded, see *Unbounded pools*.

panels.title: In use
panels.description:
**What:** connections currently checked out by queries or transactions, summed over the selected pods.

Read it together with *Free headroom*.

panels.title: Idle
panels.description:
**What:** open connections parked in the pool, ready for immediate reuse.

**Reading:** some idle connections avoid paying a handshake on every query. A large and stable idle count holds PostgreSQL connection slots for nothing (tune `SetMaxIdleConns` / `SetConnMaxIdleTime`).

panels.title: Free headroom
panels.description:
**What:** `sum(max open - in use)`: connections that can still be checked out before callers start waiting.

**Healthy:** comfortably above your usual burst size. Unlimited pools are excluded.

panels.title: DB connections held
panels.description:
**What:** `sum(open)`: physical connections Companion currently holds on the database.

**Why it matters:** this plus every other client must stay under PostgreSQL `max_connections` (minus `superuser_reserved_connections`). Compare it with your budget, especially before scaling out: each new replica can open up to `max open` more.

panels.title: Waits / s
panels.description:
**What:** rate at which callers had to wait because the pool was exhausted (`WaitCount`).

**Healthy:** 0. Any sustained value means the pool is the bottleneck and users get extra latency. See the *Contention* section.

panels.title: Avg wait time
panels.description:
**What:** `rate(wait duration) / rate(wait count)`: average time a caller waited for a connection, counting only callers that waited.

**Healthy:** no waits at all, or a few ms. Above 100 ms, users feel it: this time adds to every affected request.

panels.title: Unbounded pools
panels.description:
**What:** number of pods with `max open = 0`, i.e. `SetMaxOpenConns` never called.

**Healthy:** 0. An unbounded pool can open as many connections as there are concurrent requests and exhaust PostgreSQL during a traffic spike. Saturation can't be computed for these pods.

panels.title: Saturation: is any pod running out of connections?
Saturation per pod
panels.description:
**What:** `in use / max open` for each pod.

**Healthy:** below the orange line (70 %).

**If one pod is high and the others aren't:** look for slow queries or long transactions on that pod, uneven load balancing (sticky sessions, long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections), or a connection leak.

**If all pods rise together:** real capacity need. Scale out or raise `max open`, within the PostgreSQL connection budget.

panels.title: Free headroom per pod
panels.description:
**What:** `max open - in use` for each pod: connections still available before callers start waiting.

**Reading:** a pod at 0 is saturated *right now*; its next queries wait (see *Contention*). A line that stays flat at 0 while traffic is low suggests leaked connections.

panels.title: Pool composition: $application
panels.description:
**What:** for one application, summed over the selected pods: *in use* and *idle* stacked (their sum is *open*), with the *max open* ceiling as a dashed line.

**Reading:**
- *In use* touching *max*: saturation, callers will wait.
- *Idle* large and flat: connections kept open for nothing, holding PostgreSQL slots.
- *Max* changing: the pool configuration or the number of replicas changed.

Pods with an unlimited pool (`max open = 0`) count in *in use*/*idle* but add nothing to *max open*.

One panel is repeated per selected application.

panels.title: Contention: are requests waiting for a connection?
Waits per second per pod
panels.description:
**What:** how often callers on each pod found the pool exhausted and had to wait.

**Healthy:** a flat line at 0.

**If not:** match it with *Saturation per pod*. Waits always come with saturation near 100 % on the same pod.

panels.title: Average wait time per pod
panels.description:
**What:** average time a waiting caller spent blocked before getting a connection.

**Reading:** this latency adds directly to the response time of the affected requests. Compare it with your latency SLO: 50 ms of pool wait on a 200 ms budget is a big share.

Empty when nothing waited, which is the healthy case.

panels.title: Requests blocked on the pool (average)
panels.description:
**What:** `rate(wait_duration_seconds_total)` in seconds of waiting per second. By Little's law this equals the **average number of requests blocked waiting for a connection** at any given time.

**Example:** 3 means that, on average, 3 requests are stuck waiting on that pod at any moment. Each of them is a goroutine holding memory and a client waiting.

panels.title: Connection lifecycle: is the pool churning?
Connections closed per second, by reason
panels.description:
**What:** connections closed by the pool itself:
- **max lifetime:** reached `SetConnMaxLifetime` (planned recycling, e.g. to follow DNS changes or failovers);
- **max idle:** closed by the idle policy (see the metric note in *Reference*).

**Reading:** a steady low rate is expected. Each closed connection usually gets replaced by a new one, which costs a TCP + TLS + auth handshake on PostgreSQL.

panels.title: Estimated connection lifetime
panels.description:
**What:** `open / closure rate` (Little's law): roughly how long a connection lives before the pool recycles it.

**Healthy:** of the order of your `SetConnMaxLifetime` (typically minutes). **Seconds** means churn: the pool keeps closing connections it then reopens. Usually the cause is `SetMaxIdleConns` set too low for a bursty load, or an idle time that is too short.

*Estimate only:* it counts only the two closure reasons exported, and assumes a steady state.

panels.title: Open connections per pod
panels.description:
**What:** connections established by each pod (in use + idle).

**Reading:** the stacked total is what Companion costs PostgreSQL in connection slots. Steps up and down usually come from deployments and scaling events.

panels.title: Current state per pod
panels.description: Live snapshot of every pod, busiest first. Click a column header to re-sort. A pod with an empty *Saturation* cell has an unlimited pool (`max open = 0`).

options.content:
#### Metrics (from Go `sql.DBStats`, exposed by Companion)
| Metric | Type | `sql.DBStats` field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mpg_db_pool_max_open_connections` | gauge | `MaxOpenConnections` | Configured ceiling (`SetMaxOpenConns`). 0 = unlimited. |
| `mpg_db_pool_open_connections` | gauge | `OpenConnections` | Established connections, in use + idle. |
| `mpg_db_pool_in_use_connections` | gauge | `InUse` | Connections checked out by a query or transaction. |
| `mpg_db_pool_idle_connections` | gauge | `Idle` | Open connections waiting in the pool. |
| `mpg_db_pool_wait_count_total` | counter | `WaitCount` | Times a caller had to wait because the pool was exhausted. |
| `mpg_db_pool_wait_duration_seconds_total` | counter | `WaitDuration` | Total time spent waiting for a connection. |
| `mpg_db_pool_max_lifetime_closed_total` | counter | `MaxLifetimeClosed` | Connections closed by `SetConnMaxLifetime`. |
| `mpg_db_pool_max_idle_closed_total` | counter | `MaxIdleClosed` or `MaxIdleTimeClosed` ⚠️ | See note below. |

⚠️ In Go these are two distinct counters: `MaxIdleClosed` (pool shrinking because of `SetMaxIdleConns`) and `MaxIdleTimeClosed` (`SetConnMaxIdleTime`). The metric's help text mentions `SetConnMaxIdleTime` but its name matches `MaxIdleClosed`. Check which field the code really exports.
